title: A time for everything (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)
hook: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to weep and to laugh

segments.voice: Yesterday, God spoke to Job out of the storm, with stars and ravens and the wild ass, and no explanation. Your line was the whirlwind answered. What did you look at outdoors? Day four hundred thirty-three.

In December 1965 the number one song in America was a folk-rock record by a band called the Byrds. The folk singer Pete Seeger had written it a few years earlier, and almost every word of it was lifted straight out of the Bible, from a book that says, over and over, that everything is vapor. Millions of people sang along to an ancient list without knowing where it came from. The book is Ecclesiastes. The list is in chapter three. And it's a list that anyone who has lived a few years recognizes immediately.
screen: `NUMBER ONE IN DECEMBER 1965.` → `ALMOST EVERY WORD FROM THE BIBLE.` → `ECCLESIASTES, CHAPTER THREE.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "All things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven." Then fourteen pairs, each one a time to do something and a time to do its opposite. A time to be born and a time to die. A time to plant and a time to pull up. A time to weep and a time to laugh. A time to mourn and a time to dance. A time to embrace and a time to keep away from embraces. A time to keep silence and a time to speak. A time of war and a time of peace. Twenty-eight times, a whole life in pairs. Notice it's not a to-do list. Nobody chooses a time to die, or a time of war. It's a description: life comes in seasons, and you are always standing in one of them. The Hebrew word for time, et, means the right moment, the fitting time. So the list isn't saying everything happens; it's saying everything has its moment. A few verses later the writer says God has made everything good in its time, and has set the world, or eternity, in human hearts, and yet we can't find out the whole work of God from beginning to end. We feel the bigger shape; we only ever see our own season of it. And who is the writer? The Hebrew calls him Qoheleth, a puzzling name that seems to mean one who gathers an assembly. The Greek translated that as Ecclesiastes, from ekklesia, assembly, the same word that later meant church. Catholics often hear this passage at funerals. It doesn't rush grief. It just says: this, too, has its time.
screen: `ALL THINGS HAVE THEIR SEASON.` · `FOURTEEN PAIRS, TWENTY-EIGHT TIMES.` · `NOT A TO-DO LIST: A DESCRIPTION.` · `QOHELETH, ONE WHO GATHERS.` · then, large: `A TIME TO WEEP, AND A TIME TO LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the season you're in. Settle, and breathe. Go through a few of the pairs slowly and see which one fits right now. Is this a time to plant or a time to pull up? A time to keep silence or a time to speak? A time to embrace, or to keep a little distance? A time to mourn, or, maybe, a time to dance? You might be in more than one. Don't judge the season. Just name it, the way you'd say it's autumn. If you pray, you can offer God the season you're in, and ask to live it well. The bell holds the time.
A time for everything. Ecclesiastes' list of fourteen pairs, from birth and death to war and peace: every season of a life has its moment under heaven. Today's word.
Your line: a time for every purpose. Today, when something feels out of season, say to yourself which time this is, and let it be that. Day four hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 3 is among the Old Testament readings Catholic families may choose for a funeral, and it is also read at weekday Mass.

original.note: Hebrew: time, the fitting moment. it appears twenty-nine times in Ecclesiastes 3:1–8.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sixties song.
what it means: an ancient list of fourteen pairs saying every part of a life, joy and grief alike, has its season under heaven.
what a scholar hears: et, the fitting time; Qoheleth, the gatherer, rendered Ecclesiastes from ekklesia; and 3:11's olam, world or eternity, set in the human heart.

Turn! Turn! Turn!: written by Pete Seeger (late 1950s), the Byrds' version reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in December 1965. Confirm. The script names the song's makers but quotes none of its lyrics.
The hook says 'an ancient list' rather than giving an age: tradition ascribes the book to Solomon, while most scholars date it much later (c. 4th–3rd century BC).
Count of 'et' in 3:1–8: 29 (once in 3:1, twenty-eight in 3:2–8). Confirm.
Ecclesiastes 3:1–11 as an Old Testament option in the Order of Christian Funerals: confirm.
